article.title: Why ‘More Customers’ Does Not Always Mean ‘More Growth’
article.why: Separate customer-count growth from customer-value growth.

paragraphs.en:
A company may celebrate because its customer count increased from 1 million to 1.1 million. That sounds like clear growth. But more customers do not always mean more valuable growth. If the new customers spend little, visit rarely, or leave quickly, total customer value may not improve much.

Imagine that last year one million customers spent an average of 120,000 yen. This year the company has 1.1 million customers, but average spending falls to 100,000 yen. The customer base is 10 percent larger, yet spending per customer is lower. Total sales may still rise, but the quality of growth has changed.

The same issue appears with visit frequency. A business can add many new members through a promotion, while existing customers visit less often. Looking only at customer count hides the weakening relationship with the base.

Retention matters too. If many customers join and many others leave, the company may report a larger ending population even though loyalty is poor. That is why growth analysis should separate customer count, spending per customer, visit frequency, retention, and customer mix.

A simple report can show both scale and quality: ‘Active customers increased 10%, while annual spend per customer fell 6% and retention declined 2 percentage points.’ This gives a more complete picture than saying only, ‘Customers increased 10%.’

More customers can be good news, but the next question should be: what kind of customers were added, and how much value do they create over time?

This is especially important for membership programs. A large acquisition campaign can increase registered accounts without increasing active buyers. Some people may register only for a coupon and never return. Others may make one small purchase and become inactive. If management sees only the number of members, it may overestimate the strength of the customer base.

For better decisions, track new customers separately from retained customers and compare their spending, frequency, and survival over several months. Growth is healthier when both the number of customers and the value of their relationship improve.
paragraphs.zh:
公司可能因顧客數從100萬增加到110萬而慶祝，乍看之下是明確成長。但更多顧客不一定代表更有價值的成長。若新顧客消費少、來店低頻、或很快流失，整體 customer value 未必改善。

例如去年100萬名顧客平均年消費12萬日圓，今年顧客增至110萬，但平均降至10萬。顧客基盤擴大10%，但每人消費下降。總銷售可能仍成長，可是 growth quality 已改變。

來店頻率也是如此。促銷可以帶來大量新會員，同時既有顧客來店變少；只看 customer count 會掩蓋既有關係的弱化。

Retention 也重要。若大量新客加入、同時大量舊客流失，期末顧客總數仍可能增加，但 loyalty 並不好。因此 growth analysis 應拆開 customer count、spend per customer、visit frequency、retention 與 customer mix。

報告可以同時呈現規模與品質，例如「Active customers +10%，annual spend per customer -6%，retention -2 percentage points」。這比只說顧客增加10%更完整。

會員制度尤其需要注意。大型 acquisition campaign 可以增加註冊帳號，卻未必增加 active buyer；有人只為 coupon 註冊後就不再回來。若管理層只看會員數，會高估 customer base 的健康程度。

因此應把新客與 retained customers 分開，追蹤幾個月的 spending、frequency 與 survival。真正健康的 growth，是顧客數與關係價值一起改善。
paragraphs.ja:
顧客数が100万人から110万人へ増えると、明確な成長に見えます。しかし顧客数増加が必ずしも価値あるgrowthを意味するわけではありません。新規顧客の利用額が低い、来店頻度が低い、すぐ離脱する場合、customer valueはあまり改善しません。

例えば前年100万人が平均12万円使い、当年110万人になった一方で平均利用額が10万円へ下がれば、顧客基盤は10％拡大しても一人当たり価値は低下しています。売上総額は伸びてもgrowth qualityは変化しています。

来店頻度も同様です。promotionで新規会員が増えても既存顧客の来店が減っていれば、customer countだけでは関係の弱まりを見落とします。

retentionも重要です。加入が多くても離脱が多ければ、期末顧客数は増えてもloyaltyは弱い可能性があります。したがってcustomer count、spend per customer、frequency、retention、customer mixを分けて見る必要があります。

「Active customersは10％増、一人当たり年間利用額は6％減、retentionは2ポイント低下」のように規模と質を並べると、より完全な説明になります。

membership programでは特に重要で、大規模acquisition campaignにより登録会員は増えてもactive buyerが増えない場合があります。coupon目的で登録して戻らない人もいます。

新規顧客とretained customerを分け、数か月のspending、frequency、survivalを比較すると、顧客数と関係価値の両方が改善しているか確認できます。

vocabulary.usage: Retention can fall even when customer count rises.
Some new members quickly become inactive.
Growth can reflect a change in customer mix.

business.term: Customer-count growth and customer-value growth are not the same thing.
business.explanation: 區分規模成長與價值成長。

sources: Customer growth decomposition, retention, frequency, and value-per-customer analysis.
